#8876. Lapalma presents a cross-section of its catalogue on Dezeen Showroom

From colour palettes and modular seating to outdoor furniture and tables, Italian brand Lapalma has listed a selection of its most recent products on our Showroom section.

The brand collaborated with architect and designer Raffaella Mangiarotti on a new palette of colourways that can be applied across its offering of products.

Nine new shades join seven rethought existing colours in what the brand describes as a “chromatic alphabet”, which can be mixed or matched across seating, tables and accessories.

When designing the collection, Mangiarotti considered each colour’s capacity to work seamlessly whether applied to metal, wood or plastic.

The brand’s Kipu Club outdoor chair presents a new iteration of Anderssen & Voll‘s original design and can withstand life outdoors.

A curvilinear backrest partially wraps a pebble-shaped seat, creating a comfortable and friendly seat for al fresco lounging.

A family of tables have been developed for the brand by designer Mario Ferrarini, who created and named the collection after the conical profile of Mount Kilimanjaro.

Aptly named Kili, the tables are designed to be sculptural as well as functional, coming in various sizes and tabletop shapes, with each element carefully aesthetically considered.

Snaking lengths of seating are created in this new modular system designed for the brand by Francesco Rota, who wanted to make “welcoming islands for meeting, working, waiting or simply taking a pause”.

The HUB modular system is reconfigurable, allowing users to reorder the modules to create evolving landscapes in open-plan spaces.

Designer Francesco Rota collaborated with Lapalma to extend the Plus modular outdoor seating system, which now comprises additional sun loungers and facilitates all-new combination options.

Round-cornered, lozenge-shaped modules available in various bright and neutral-coloured upholstery make up the range, which creates opportunity for open-air lounging and socialising.

Lapalma is an Italian furniture company with a forty-year history of designing and manufacturing tables, seating and other furnishings for both indoor and outdoor use.

#8875. Does Magnesium Help You Lose Belly Fat?

We include products we think are useful for our readers. If you buy through links on this page, we may earn a small commission. Here’s our process

Magnesium is found in fatty fish, leafy greens, whole grains — and the supplement aisle.

The mighty mineral plays many essential roles in our bodies, but can it help tighten the belt buckle?

While magnesium can sneakily support weight loss in a few ways, that’s not its main gig.

“Magnesium alone is not a magic bullet for weight loss,” says Paunel Vukasinov, MD, a dual board-certified internist and obesity medicine specialist with Medical Offices of Manhattan.

“A comprehensive approach including diet, exercise, and other lifestyle changes are essential,” Vukasinov adds.

Here are a few ways magnesium may support weight loss, as explained by Vukasinov.

“Magnesium is not classified as an appetite suppressant,” Vukasinov says.

“However, by potentially stabilizing blood sugar and insulin levels, magnesium may reduce cravings and help prevent overeating. This effect can indirectly support weight loss.”

Vukasinov reminds us that no specific magnesium dosage is prescribed solely for fat loss.

With that in mind, the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for magnesium is:

Vukasinov says that sticking to the RDA ensures you meet your body’s needs without over-supplementing.

“Excessive intake does not enhance weight loss and may lead to adverse effects,” he adds.

According to Vukasinov, it’s best to get magnesium from food since a nutrient-dense diet, including whole foods, boosts your intake of other extra essentials like fiber, which improves overall health.

Here are some foods you can gobble up for the most magnesium:

If you know your diet isn’t cutting it, you can find magnesium supplements at major retailers, like Wal-Mart and Target, drug stores, or Amazon.

PSA: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not check the safety or effectiveness of dietary supplements, so it’s important to choose a reputable brand that undertakes third-party testing to prove the purity and quality of their products.

For some, magnesium supplements may cause a few unsavory side effects, including diarrhea, stomach upset, or cramping.

Remember that there are many forms of magnesium. Vukasinov points out that magnesium citrate or magnesium oxide can have a laxative effect (yikes).

Be sure you’re taking the best dose based on your RDA, and consider taking it with a meal to better avoid side effects.

Magnesium is not a miracle solution for weight loss, but getting enough of it can ensure that your body produces enough energy and gets enough sleep — both play a big hand in weight management.

Taking too much will have you gripping your belly with stomach pain or diarrhea, so stick to the daily recommended amounts.

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024

#8874. How Taking a GLP-1 Could Affect Your Bone Health

When it comes to treating obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic health conditions, GLP-1 agonist drugs—such as Ozempic, Zepbound, and Wegovy—have been a game changer for literally millions of Americans.

But as with any medication, these drugs can deliver unwelcome side effects. And a recent study that just garnered a bunch of attention raised the possibility of new ones.

The research, which was presented at the 2026 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons annual meeting in March and has not yet been peer-reviewed, found a link between GLP-1 use and increased risk of bone issues, including osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) and osteomalacia (soft bones). The study also found a link between GLP-1 use and heightened risk of gout, a type of arthritis that causes pain and swelling in the joints.

The lead study author said he became interested in whether GLP-1s might affect bone and other connective tissue after some of his patients “developed serious tendon tears following relatively minor injuries,” according to NBC News. After analyzing five years of medical records from nearly 147,000 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity, the study authors concluded that GLP-1 use was associated with a “significantly increased” risk of osteoporosis, osteomalacia, and gout.

Of course, this news is likely unsettling for anyone on these medications. But should we be legit worried about these findings? And how exactly could GLP-1s harm bone health in the first place? We tapped two experts for answers, along with practical tips for protecting bone health while taking GLP-1s.

First, some relieving news: As of now, there is “no sound scientific evidence” that suggests GLP-1s directly increase the risk of osteoporosis or osteomalacia, Marci Laudenslager, MD, an obesity medicine physician with The Johns Hopkins Healthful Eating, Activity & Weight Program, tells SELF. (Same goes for gout, she adds.)

Dr. Laudenslager, who was not involved in the study, points out that it was observational in nature, meaning it looked at correlation…not causation. “While well-conducted observational studies can reveal a potential relationship between a medication and a clinical outcome, they cannot determine whether a medication directly causes that clinical outcome,” she explains.

Another limitation of the study is that it relied on medical records alone, which means it assumed that all patients who were prescribed GLP-1s, as noted in their medical records, were actually taking the drug. In reality, many patients who are prescribed GLP-1s are unable to take them because of cost or medication shortages, Dr. Laudenslager says. Moreover, people who do start taking don’t always continue due to insurance, cost, or problems tolerating the drug, she adds.

Beyond that, the study didn’t take into account factors that commonly impact bone health, like exercise habits, nutritional habits, and other lifestyle factors, Kelyssa Hall, an exercise physiologist and certified strength and conditioning specialist at Hospital for Special Surgery, tells SELF. “These factors can play a huge role in bone health with or without the addition of GLP-1s.” The study also didn’t account for certain endocrine conditions, cancers, alcohol use, family history, and steroid use–all of which can also play a role in bone health, Dr. Laudenslager adds. And the study didn’t note which specific GLP-1 drug people used and the dosage, she adds.

Lastly, the study findings have not yet been peer reviewed–a step that Dr. Laudenslager describes it as “essential” in the scientific process. As Hall puts it: The study “highlights the need for more research on these topics.”

Okay, so that particular study has its limitations. But other research supports the notion that these drugs may be linked with declining bone health. So…is there actual cause for concern?

According to Dr. Laudenslager and Hall, taking GLP1-s can indeed decrease bone density for some people. But that’s likely due to the volume and rate at which people lose weight while on these drugs—and not anything specific to the medication itself, Dr. Laudenslager says.

“When you take GLP-1s, there can be rapid weight loss which means there is less load being carried around on the skeleton,” Hall says. “Bone formation or strengthening is improved with load to the skeletal system,” she explains, “so losing weight decreases the regular load on the bones overall.”

Over time, this decrease in loading can translate to a decrease in bone density, Dr. Laudenslager says. But, again, this isn’t unique to GLP-1s: “Significant weight loss through any mechanism—lifestyle change, medications, or surgery—can impact metabolism as a whole and bone metabolism, in particular,” she says. Basically, whenever you lose a bunch of weight—regardless of how you lost those pounds—there’s always a risk of bone loss.

In short, while it’s true that some people taking GLP-1s have had changes to their bone health, these changes seem to “be driven primarily by magnitude of weight loss rather than a direct, negative consequence of the medications themselves,” Dr. Laudenslager says. That said, the use of GLP-1s and bone health “is an active area of study,” she adds. More research is needed to fully understand the impact of GLP-1s on bone density.

Resistance training is important for pretty much everyone—and that includes folks on GLP-1s. One of its many benefits is that it’s been shown to improve bone density, Hall says. That means it can be a helpful strategy to bolster bone health when you’re on a GLP-1. Plus, strength training can help guard against muscle loss that can happen when you’re losing weight. “Retaining muscle mass is important for strength and stability,” she says. And it can also help support your overall metabolism, she adds, which can help your body sustain weight loss results for the long haul.

If you’re new to strength training, Dr. Laudenslager recommends gradually building up to a routine of two to three sessions a week, with at least a day off in between each workout to allow your muscles the time they need to recover. Before getting started though, make sure to check with your doctor or other medical provider so they can advise what type of workouts are safe and recommended for you.

A common side effect of GLP-1s is appetite suppression, which can sometimes lead people to follow a really low calorie diet. Calorie restriction can suppress bone growth and increase the risk of fractures, according to research, which is one of the reasons you want to make sure you’re still eating enough to support your overall health while on a GLP-1. “Hunger is an essential hormonal cue we all need in order to sustain health,” Dr. Laudenslager says. The ideal amount of calories is highly individualized, but if you’re unsure that you’re getting what you need, bring it up with your doctor or another qualified expert, such as a registered dietitian.

Protein is often touted for its muscle-building benefits, but it’s also vital for bone health, as it helps to build bone mass. The recommended dietary allowance for adults is 0.8 grams of protein per kilograms of bodyweight a day—a general guideline that Dr. Laudenslager also suggests for people taking GLP-1s. She suggests a slightly higher intake for people at greater risk of bone health issues (such as older adults and postmenopausal women) and lesser amounts in people with kidney disease. Just make sure that as you prioritize protein, you don’t skimp on important components of a well-rounded diet, including fiber, water, healthy fats, and essential vitamins, minerals, and nutrients, she adds.

Rapid weight loss can be harmful for bone health, so to mitigate this risk, strive for a more gradual reduction in pounds. The recommended rate of weight loss depends on your starting weight, but as a general guideline, Dr. Laudenslager recommends losing 5% to 10% of your total weight over the course of about six months. This translates to an average of about 0.5 to 2 pounds lost a week. So if you notice that taking a GLP-1 is causing you to lose weight at a faster pace, bring it up with your doctor. They may want to adjust your medication dosing to help slow your weight loss rate into a more ideal, gradual range.

Bone loss isn’t an overnight thing. In fact, clinically significant bone loss typically happens over the course of years, Dr. Laudenslager says. “This means there are a wealth of opportunities throughout a person’s weight loss journey to prevent and treat bone loss early on if it’s detected through surveillance.” So if you have any bone health concerns, mention them to your doctor (though hopefully your provider is proactively thinking about this too).

On that note, Dr. Laudenslager strongly encourages people interested in obesity treatment to seek care from a board-certified obesity medicine physician. She recommends the American Board of Obesity Medicine and the Obesity Action Coalition websites as resources for finding a board-certified provider.

GLP-1s can be a true game-changer for people struggling with chronic health conditions. Unfortunately, there’s still a lot of societal stigma and misunderstanding surrounding obesity, including the misconception that “anti-obesity medications are dangerous and should be avoided,” Dr. Laudenslager says. #8873. Ontario house by Brian O'Brian takes cues from farm buildings

Canadian architect Brian O’Brian has completed a rural weekend house in Ontario that features a slanted, corrugated-metal facade and an angled roof covered with greenery.

The Hemlock House sits on a 72-acre (29-hectare) property in the southern town of Markdale.

The project grew in scope over time. Originally, the plan was to renovate an old farmhouse, but the client ultimately decided to create an entirely new house.

“What started as a modest renovation evolved into a full replacement of the small, 1930s farmhouse,” said Brian O’Brian, a Toronto-based architect.

The commission came about after the client saw another project by O’Brian in the area – a 19th-century schoolhouse with stone walls that had been converted into a cottage.

For the Hemlock House, O’Brian took cues from the region’s agrarian buildings to conceive the design.

Set on a flat site surrounded by woods and farmland, the house is composed of a long bar and adjoining box, and totals 3,250 square feet (302 square metres).

A long entry driveway “traces the lineage of the site”, passing by an old farmhouse and century-old barn.

The new house draws upon these earlier buildings and “extends the language of agricultural buildings into a contemporary domestic form”, the architect said.

The home’s bar-shaped volume is topped with a sloped, metal-clad roof, while the attached box has an angular green roof.

The north side of the house is lined with a slanted wall made of corrugated metal.

Cut into the wall are three windows, which can be covered by external, perforated steel panels that slide up and down. This elevation also features a boxy protrusion with wood cladding.

“This is meant to feel like an agrarian building at first view, but one that begins softening and opening on approach,” said the architect.

The southern elevation – which overlooks patios and a swimming pool – features hemlock siding and ample glazing. Various roof overhangs help shield the building from sun and snow.

The house also has a carport, which is sheltered by a canopy made of wood and metal.

Within the home, there is a division between public and private spaces.

The linear volume, which spans two levels, contains a principal suite, a secondary suite, and two bedrooms with a shared bathroom. The adjoining box holds a kitchen, dining area and living room.

Rooms feature neutral colours and a mix of earthy and industrial materials.

“Concrete and hemlock define every surface, carrying a steady material logic through the house,” the architect said.

Other projects in Ontario include a 1970s chalet that was renovated and expanded by UUfie to conform to its steep site, and a black cabin by Barbora Vokac Taylor that includes wedge-shaped clerestory windows.

#8870. Concept car that transforms from SUV to pickup is "a symbol of freedom" says Fiat CEO

Fiat’s new Multiplay concept car can transform from an SUV into a pickup, with movable seats and a flexible interior designed to accommodate different uses, explains the brand’s CEO Arnaud Belloni in this exclusive video interview produced by Dezeen.

“We are reinventing here the concept of family car,” said Belloni, describing the vehicle, which was unveiled at the 2026 Paris Motor Show.

Measuring 4.45 metres long, Multiplay combines the passenger space of a multi-purpose vehicle (MPV) with the raised stance of an SUV and the open cargo area of a pickup.

A sliding rear section allows the vehicle to switch between configurations, changing its enclosed passenger compartment into an open load bed.

The concept takes inspiration from the original Fiat 600 Multipla, launched in 1956, which accommodated six people within a body measuring just 3.5 metres long.

“Basically, that car invented the concept of multipurpose vehicle – the MPV,” said Belloni, referring to the original model.

The new Multiplay revisits this approach through a series of movable components. Its seats can be repositioned to accommodate different passenger and cargo arrangements, while the rear spoiler rotates to become an integrated bicycle rack capable of carrying two bikes.

“Multiplay can slide from an MPV to an SUV to a pickup,” said Belloni. “That, I would say, is a symbol of freedom.”

In its family configuration, the car accommodates six passengers alongside an additional modular seat.

The pickup configuration provides an open load bed for carrying bicycles, sports equipment and other bulky items.

Inside, a multifunctional unit called the Petsenger seat can be used to accommodate a pet, mount a child car seat or serve as a small table.

The front passenger seat can also turn towards the rear to create a reclining Sunseat, which uses the dashboard as a backrest and sits beneath a panoramic roof.

The interior uses a contrasting palette of red and pink, set against bright green exterior bodywork inspired by the colours of a watermelon.

Its textiles were made using a stitch-free, three-dimensional knitting process, while a digital display integrated into the dashboard disappears when the vehicle is switched off.

Multiplay was presented alongside Multiplina, a separate three-metre-long electric concept with four seats and two doors, as part of Fiat‘s wider exploration of urban and family transportation at the car show.

The company describes Multiplay as a testing ground for future design solutions rather than a preview of a specific production model.

“Fiat is obsessed with all types of mobility on each size of car. So whatever the size, we are able to invent new categories of vehicles,” said Belloni.

Founded in Turin in 1899, Fiat is an Italian automotive manufacturer producing passenger cars and commercial vehicles, from compact city cars to larger family vehicles.

#8869. How to Use Jojoba Oil for Hair: Expert Tips for Stunning Results

Jojoba oil is a must-have for moisturizing shampoos and skincare products.

The slippery oil is squeezed out of jojoba plant seeds. These plants are shrubs that pop up around the desert-y spots ofArizona, southern California, and Mexico.

Though it’s been used as a natural remedy for centuries, jojoba oil is having a major hair moment right now.

Keep reading to learn how to use it for strong, shiny hair and a healthy scalp.

“Jojoba oil is incredibly nourishing,” says Mayara Macedo, a hairstylist and scalp specialist in NYC. “It’s a natural oil that closely resembles the sebum our skin and scalp produce,” Macedo explains.

Because of this, Macedo says it’s super compatible with our bodies and works great as a balancing treatment — whether you have an oily or dry scalp.

While its proven benefits mainly revolve around its help with scalp health, jojoba oil can also strengthen and moisturize hair. However, it’s not the go-to pick for improving hair loss (that’s usually minoxidil).

If you’re dealing with dryness, jojoba oil is fantastic for adding moisture to your scalp,” Macedo says.

“Its natural hydrating properties help restore balance, leaving everything healthier and more manageable.”

“Jojoba oil has been known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties in addition to its conditioning and emollient properties,” says Kseniya Kobets, MD, board-certified dermatologist and Director of Cosmetics Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care.

These properties help out with dry, irritating dandruff.

This also explains jojoba oil‘s Mexican Indian history as a treatment for sores, which eventually caused researchers to flag its potential for improving skin conditions like acne and psoriasis (but please see a dermatologist for proven treatment options).

Though many say that jojoba oil grows hair, this claim is probably tossed around because it helps moisturize hair follicles — which can keep dryness at bay.

A dry environment can be a breeding ground for breakage, hair loss, and dandruff.

Also, your split ends say hello — jojoba oil can help by restoring hair health overall.

“If your scalp gets oily quickly after washing,” Macedo says, “It could be because your scalp is overcompensating, thinking it doesn’t have enough moisture and needs to produce more oil.”

She says adding jojoba oil helps signal to your scalp that it has enough, which can slow down excess oil production.

Although you can apply jojoba oil to the length and tips of your hair, Macedo says she prefers to use it only for the scalp, saying that other oils, like argan oil, will work better for the length.

Here;s how Macedo recommends using jojoba oil:

You can also buy shampoos or conditions that already have it!

Macedo says you can apply jojoba oil to wet or dry hair, depending on your goal.

“If you want to lock in moisture and add shine, you can try applying it to damp hair.” However, she doesn’t recommend this because it’s easy to accidentally apply too much or distribute it unevenly on wet hair, which she says can leave your hair feeling heavy and greasy.

“Applying it to dry hair reduces frizz and adds a light shine to styled hair,” she suggests.

Kobets recommends using oils overnight for extended exposure. However, she points out this can get messy (RIP pillowcases), so you can always apply them for a few hours and wash them off before bed.

Macedo also suggests being mindful of the amount you use — too much can make your hair look greasy, especially true for fine hair. “For a lightweight finish, start with a small amount and focus on the ends of your hair. But again, I’d recommend jojoba oil for the scalp and argan oil for the hair,” Macedo adds.

“If you’re using jojoba oil as a pre-wash treatment to balance scalp oil or as a deep conditioner, apply it before washing,” Macedo explains. “If you’re using it as a leave-in conditioner or frizz-tamer, you can apply it to freshly washed hair — careful not to apply too much.”

Kobets suggests washing the scalp after using oils, noting that her patients don’t always prefer to use them because they can reduce hair volume for some.

Kobets says that someone with a dehydrated scalp and coarse hair may want to leave the oil in to hydrate the scalp better. “People with fine or oily scalps usually want to wash the oils out,” she adds.

Jojoba oil is a natural moisturizing ingredient known for improving scalp health. It can also add shine and help strengthen your locks.

It’s not the move for improving hair loss, however.

Do a patch test to make sure you aren’t allergic first! Then you’re good to glow.

#8868. Design Doha Biennial 2026 set to explore how traditional crafts can shape the future of design

Design Doha Biennial 2026 opens in Doha, Qatar, today, bringing together more than 19 exhibitions, five installations and over 80 designers, featuring projects that use traditional water systems and building techniques to tackle urban heat.

Following a postponement earlier this year due to war in the Gulf, the event will now run from today until 31 January 2027, with its opening programme taking place from 5 to 7 November.

For the event Doha‘s historic neighbourhood of Fereej Al Asmakh has been transformed into an exhibition venue to showcase contemporary architecture and design from across the Middle East, north Africa and south Asia.

The biennial features more than 19 exhibitions across over 20 countries, alongside five permanent public design commissions, talks and awards. Many of the exhibitions occupy restored courtyard houses in Fereej Al Asmakh, where installations sit within the neighbourhood’s existing buildings and outdoor spaces.

At the centre of the biennial is Arab Design Now 2026, a group exhibition curated by Palestinian architect Noura Al Sayeh that brings together 81 designers, artisans and makers.

The exhibition includes 78 new commissions and 17 films, presenting finished objects alongside the people, materials and processes involved in making them.

“The second edition of Arab Design Now, the headline exhibition of the Design Doha Biennial, puts context in the foreground,” said Al Sayeh.

“It showcases design alongside the designers themselves, as well as the related environments, processes, artisans, craftsmen and makers.”

Other highlights include The Sower, an exhibition by Mexican designer Fernando Laposse featuring a living seed bank developed in Qatar.

Another exhibition called Post-Oil 2026 examines how industrial materials such as concrete, glass, steel and aluminium have shaped the built environment of the Gulf.

Five public design commissions will also be installed in Fereej Al Asmakh, reinterpreting traditional construction methods and environmental techniques for contemporary urban settings.

These include Salsabil, a cooling structure by French architecture studio New South that uses ceramic spheres and fine mist to create cooler areas in public spaces, as well as Palm Construct, a shaded pavilion by Emirati architect Abdalla Almulla that combines palm wood with traditional weaving techniques.

Dezeen will be reporting from Doha throughout the opening, visiting the exhibitions and public installations to bring readers the highlights of this year’s programme.

The team will also be speaking to Design Doha director Fahad Al Obaidly and Arab Design Now curator Noura Al Sayeh, alongside participating architects and designers, to explore the ideas and processes behind the exhibitions.

Design Doha was established in 2024 by Qatar Museums under the leadership of its chairperson, Sheikha Al Mayassa bint Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani.

The inaugural edition featured more than 300 designers and studios across 24 exhibitions and attracted more than 118,000 visitors, establishing the biennial as a platform for contemporary design from the region.

Design Doha 2026 takes place from 5 November until 31 December in Doha, Qatar. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

#8867. For Some Women, Weight Loss Drugs Are a Secret They Keep From Their Partners

The first time Caroline went on Wegovy, it wasn’t a secret: She told her boyfriend, mother, and close friends. Over the course of six months, they watched as she shed 30 pounds, going from 130 back to what she calls her “healthy original weight” of 100 pounds. Even still, her loved ones worried about the extent of her weight loss and didn’t want her to lose even more.

So she went online and found a doctor who prescribed the medication over the phone, unaware of how much Caroline actually weighed. Immediately after starting Wegovy, she says, “the weight started coming off incredibly fast.” After six months she decided she wanted to stop. But as soon as she got off Wegovy, the weight came back: She gained 10 pounds in a month. “I realized, I can’t stop,” Caroline says.

So for the past six months, she has been taking Wegovy again, this time at a maintenance-level dosage. But there’s one big difference: This time, she’s keeping it a secret from her boyfriend and family. “Now that we’re talking about kids, he’s seen all the impacts [of the drug] and he’s done with it,” she says. Since she lives alone, hiding her medication from him is relatively easy—she stashes it in the back of the fridge, since it needs to be kept cold. But she’s still worried he’ll see it, and when they travel together, she has to hide the medication in the hotel room fridge—or, if they’re visiting his parents, in their refrigerator. “So imagine, I’m hiding stuff in my parents-in-laws’ fridge, hoping they won’t see them,” she says. “It’s super awkward.”

Caroline isn’t the only woman going to great lengths to keep her GLP-1 use a secret. On a recent thread on the r/GLP1microdosing subreddit, women shared their tips and tricks for hiding medication from their partners. One stashes them in a tomato paste box. Another uses a play food container from a child’s pretend kitchen. Still others have turned to an opaque feta cheese container, butter stick box, anchovy paste box, empty bottles of women’s probiotics and Alani Nu supplements, a plastic to-go container, a metal water bottle, a box of wine, and a baking soda box in the back of the fridge—all to conceal the weight loss medication.

“It’s a real thing,” Kia Mitchell, MD, who specializes in family and obesity medicine, tells SELF. She has seen numerous women in her Jacksonville, Florida, practice go to similar efforts to hide their medication from their partners. The first time she heard about this pattern, it was from a patient who “just didn’t want to turn this into a debate at home,” she says. “She just wanted to have the option” to take the medication. “A lot of my patients are similar,” Dr. Mitchell adds. “There’s this loss of control with the gaining of the weight, but being able to control the narrative around weight loss has been empowering and exciting” for her patients. “Because now they can reveal it on their own terms. That’s where the control comes back.”

The reasons women want to reveal their weight loss medications on their own terms are palpable in that subreddit thread. “If my husband found out, it would just be a series of lectures,” wrote a user called Vivid-Act-6442. “Just don’t want to hear any negative or critical opinions,” wrote another user called [deleted]. “After 52 years of marriage, one knows one’s mate.” One woman chimed in to say she was hiding her meds from her teens—because she didn’t want them telling her ex-husband. “I just don’t feel like the questions,” she wrote.

Dr. Mitchell has mixed feelings about this type of secrecy. Anyone on a health journey benefits from having a “network that’s really cheering for you,” Dr. Mitchell says. “Dealing with something like this, I want people to have community.” But, she continues, it’s “empowering and protective” for women to get to decide who knows about their weight loss drugs—even if, ideally, “you really want to be in a relationship with someone you trust completely.”

From a medical standpoint, there are some potential pitfalls to hiding GLP-1s from a significant other. For one, it’s easier to get pregnant while taking them—Mitchell says she has “several GLP-1 babies” in her practice. There are also the drugs’ potential side effects, and hiding medication can make it more difficult for a patient to turn to her partner if she’s struggling. And more generally, secrecy can cause stress. “When someone is trying to lose weight, we want their stress hormones to be as low as possible,” Dr. Mitchell says. “If you’re trying to hide [medication], we’ll be fighting an uphill battle if you’re stressed about that.”

The bigger issue is hiding GLP-1 medications from your regular doctor, something that has become much easier thanks to the rise in telehealth companies like Hers and Ro. That’s a problem Caroline is having: She didn’t tell her doctor both times she went on Wegovy and still doesn’t want to, even though she’s concerned about how the drug may interact with the Accutane and Ritalin she takes. The idea of admitting her GLP-1 use to her doctor makes her anxious, since she doesn’t want to break their trust. But her annual physical is coming up, and her doctor will see that she’s lost a lot of weight.

“I use ChatGPT as my doctor at this point since I can’t be honest with my own doctor,” she says. “I say, ‘Hey, this is my actual weight, what type of dosage is okay to take with other drugs?’” Admittedly, she adds, this is “probably not the best option.”

Caroline got her Wegovy prescription through Hers. During the process she was only asked for basic bloodwork and received no counseling, just “documentation to read.”

Craig Primack, MD, the head of weight loss at Hers, tells SELF that the company’s prescribing doctors “do ask [patients] to talk with their primary care doctor about the care they’re getting.” He acknowledges that the company doesn’t do much in the way of direct counseling but says that “we ask about mental health and anxiety and stresses.” The Hers app contains what Primack terms “psychologist-built information” about topics such as sleep management and eating personas.

Dr. Primack is “absolutely” aware that some patients hide their medication from their partners. He says that some don’t want to say anything until they’ve proven they can lose weight; some don’t want to say anything because of the medication’s cost; some worry about how it could change the way they and their partner see each other. “Your weight and persona set up a dynamic in your couple,” Dr. Primack says. “When you start changing that, sometimes spouses get very jealous—‘Oh my god, you’re becoming potentially more attractive.’ Not that weight is directly linked to that, but that’s what I hear them say.”

And then, of course, there’s the more general stigma associated with weight and weight loss. “One benefit of telemedicine is it takes the bias and stigma away,” Dr. Primack says. “One reason we are here is because people are uncomfortable going to talk to their primary care doctor about it.”

Whether or not Caroline decides to tell her doctor about her medication, she still will have to grapple with the larger issues that her Wegovy use, and her secrecy around it, have raised. “It’s very stressful,” she says. “The fact that not only can I not talk about it, but I’m also unable to get off of it. I don’t love the idea of taking medicine like that forever, but I’m kind of stuck with it.” She doesn’t want to gain weight, she explains. “But I wonder to which extent I’m too harsh with my criticism of my body. Maybe my goals are too intense.”

Given the incredible degree of vulnerability and sensitivity tied up with weight loss, the dilemma about whether to tell people about a GLP-1 medication is all too understandable. But how to tell people can make it easier, says Rachel Goldman, PhD, a clinical assistant professor in the department of psychiatry at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a clinical psychologist whose areas of expertise include weight management and disordered eating, tells SELF. “Framing it around their own experience and needs can make the conversation feel more manageable and less like something they have to defend,” she says.

Since deciding whether to have this conversation isn’t easy, Dr. Goldman would first encourage a patient to “think about their why,” she says. “What led them to this decision? What does this treatment mean for their health and wellbeing?” Once someone feels more grounded and confident in their reasoning, “it becomes easier to communicate it with that confidence.”

Dr. Goldman also suggests coming up with some sample scripts before having the conversation. “I would suggest that they lead with their own personal experience and not think about others and why/how others are using it,” she says. “I would encourage them to use ‘I’ statements.”

It’s also helpful to think ahead of time about a partner’s potential reaction and to have a plan in place for different scenarios. Thinking about what you want from a partner is likewise helpful—is it support, understanding, “or simply space to make their own health decisions without judgement?” Dr. Goldman asks. She adds that it’s important to remember that a partner’s initial reaction might not be their final reaction—it can take time for someone to process a conversation and to work through their own biases and misconceptions.

“Ultimately,” she says, “the goal isn’t to have a perfect conversation, but it’s to open the door to more honesty, connection, and support over time.”

But if that fails, there’s always a box of anchovy paste.

#8866. 6 Signs Your Skin Needs Medical Attention, Stat

Your skin is your most visible organ, so it’s easy to notice when something seems off. It’s normal to experience some skin issues from time to time, like itchiness, breakouts, or ingrown hairs. But when these skin symptoms stick around, it could be a sign that something more serious is going on.

Many of these skin issues get better with the right at-home remedies or changes in your skin care routine. For example, if dryness pops up when Old Man Winter comes along, slathering on a more intense moisturizer may help.

But if skin symptoms don’t go away with a little self-care — or they return frequently — a chronic skin condition might be the culprit. However, just because you have a lasting symptom or two doesn’t necessarily mean you have a chronic health issue.

Here are the symptoms you should watch for and what they might mean. And if they don’t improve, consider checking in with a dermatologist for a proper diagnosis and a plan of action.

If you wish you had cat claws to satisfy your skin itch, you could be dealing with eczema. Eczema is an umbrella term for several conditions that impact the skin, with atopic dermatitis being the most common.

With most forms of eczema, your skin may show signs of inflammation, such as:

These symptoms may flare up occasionally and then go into periods of remission, where your skin isn’t as irritated.

Allergies can also lead to itchiness. For example, if you’re allergic to a skin care ingredient, a fabric type, a pet, or another allergen, your skin might react as a way to tell you to avoid this trigger.

Ongoing or regular periods of itchiness are a reason to see a dermatologist.

A rash can affect the skin in various ways, including:

A one-off or temporary rash might result from friction or chafing from a new outfit item. It could also be a heat rash when sweat gets trapped in skinfolds or bodily creases.

A persistent rash could be a sign of eczema or allergies. However, different types of rashes can be a sign of other things. For example, a butterfly-shaped (malar) rash across the face is a common sign of an autoimmune disease known as lupus.

If you frequently experience skin rashes, talk with a dermatologist to help you get to the bottom of the issue.

Dry skin can be just that — dry skin. Common causes include:

But if your skin is so dry it makes you want to bathe in a vat of thick moisturizer, it could be a sign of psoriasis.

Psoriasis is an inflammatory skin condition potentially caused by an overactive immune system. It can lead to dry, cracked, or scaling skin. In fact, psoriasis often involves a buildup of scales or plaques on areas like the elbows or knees — though they can occur anywhere.

Psoriasis and eczema are different conditions, but they have overlapping symptoms that mimic each other. So if you experience these symptoms, it’s important to see a dermatologist to identify and treat the underlying cause.

Changes in skin color — including red, brown, gray, or purple patches of skin — can be a sign of various skin issues, including eczema, psoriasis, or allergies. But it can also be a sign of rosacea.

Rosacea typically involves persistent redness that looks like a sunburn or blushing. It may also lead to skin thickening.

The good news? Rosacea is highly treatable. So working with a dermatologist can help you address it.

No one is immune from developing the occasional pimple or ingrown hair. But sometimes, skin bumps can be a sign that something else is going on.

Acne is one of the most common skin conditions that could bring skin bumps like pimples.

Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is another condition that causes painful, boil-like lumps to form underneath the skin. These bumps can turn into pus-filled pockets that may connect via tunnels. HS typically shows up in areas of high friction or where skin meets skin, such as the armpits or groin.

Other types of skin bumps may include ingrown hairs, which can get infected and turn into folliculitis.

Talk with a dermatologist to help you address any bothersome skin bumps you may experience.

Common moles are growths that develop when pigment cells (melanocytes) grow in clusters. The average adult has between 10 to 40 common moles.

An irregular mole, also known as a dysplastic nevus, is a type of mole that looks different from your common moles. If you have a dysplastic nevus (or several), schedule regular skin checks with a dermatologist to look for anything suspicious. Be sure to mention any changes in:

These types of changes could be a sign of a form of skin cancer such as melanoma, which occurs in melanocytes. Melanoma can develop anywhere, including on normal-looking skin, a common mole, or a dysplastic nevus.

Skin symptoms — like rashes, bumps, discoloration, dryness, or itchiness — may come and go. But if symptoms stick around or return frequently, consider seeing a dermatologist for an evaluation. Your skin may be telling you that there’s an underlying issue that needs to be addressed.

A dermatologist can provide a proper diagnosis and treatment plan to help reduce, or, in some cases, resolve your skin symptoms. If you don’t currently have a dermatologist, your primary care physician or nurse practitioner can refer you to one.

#8865. "Commitment of the design community remains strong" say Ukrainian design week founders

Photography courtesy of Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week

This year’s Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week went ahead despite Russian strikes affecting the local design community. The event’s founders share their top picks of exhibited brands that have continued production amid the war.

“The reality of operating in Ukraine remains extremely challenging,” Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week founders Anatolii and Kateryna Roskovshenko told Dezeen.

Ukraine has endured the constant threat of Russian bombardment for over four years, and recent months have been increasingly deadly for civilians, according to Human rights group Amnesty International.

Daily life for Ukrainians continues to be upended. Designers and manufacturers are navigating keeping operations running as Russian strikes damage their warehouses.

“Air raid alerts, power outages, disrupted logistics, rising costs, and damage to production facilities directly affect everyday operations,” said the husband-and-wife duo. “Several major Ukrainian furniture manufacturers have had their production facilities and warehouses hit by Russian strikes, causing significant damage and disrupting their work.”

“Businesses often have to adjust their schedules at short notice, reconsider investments, and find alternative ways to maintain production. Some have been forced to scale back operations or temporarily suspend projects,” they continued.

In the face of this, the design community came together for this year’s Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week, which took place in Kyiv from 5 to 11 October.

The flagship Design Hall exhibition gathered two hundred Ukrainian brands across interiors, furniture, decor, lighting and product design, showcasing their work to thousands of visitors.

Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week, which joined the international community of World Design Weeks in 2023, made changes to its planned programme to keep attendees safe. During the event, Kyiv experienced attacks that interrupted electricity and water supplies.

“Several planned events had to be cancelled for security reasons, while some furniture brands were unable to participate following earlier attacks on their facilities,” said the Roskovshenkos.

“We adapted Design Hall to take place entirely indoors, with changes to the original programme.”

“Yet the commitment of the design community remains strong,” they continued. “Thousands of people attended Design Hall, and hundreds of designers, manufacturers, and creative professionals came together to exchange ideas, establish new connections, and support each other’s work.”

Design brands in Ukraine are exploring new ways of developing products, testing materials and reaching customers, according to the Roskovshenkos.

“Despite the challenges of working during the war, Ukraine’s design industry continues to evolve,” they said. “Collaboration has become an essential part of how the industry operates, helping businesses share knowledge, find new opportunities, and adapt to uncertainty.”

“Particularly encouraging is the fact that new Ukrainian design brands continue to launch, even as existing businesses navigate difficult circumstances.”

“Over seven seasons of Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week, we have witnessed this evolution firsthand,” the pair continued. “Brands are becoming more confident in their identity, finding new niches, rethinking their production processes, and developing products that reflect their own creative vision.”

Read on for Anatolii and Kateryna Roskovshenko’s highlights from this year’s Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week:

“Juniper is a Ukrainian brand that combines traditional Carpathian craftsmanship with contemporary design, working with natural materials such as sheep’s wool and wood.

“In collaboration with KredoBank, the brand has created a collection of four wall panels inspired by Ukraine’s distinctive landscapes.

“Through natural textures and handcrafted techniques, each piece captures the character and atmosphere of these places, bringing elements of Ukraine’s cultural and natural heritage into contemporary interiors.”

“Gushka is a Ukrainian wool textile manufacturer [that] preserves traditional craftsmanship, creating its products on historic weaving looms using age-old techniques and natural wool from sheep that graze freely on the Carpathian slopes.

“Kint is a Kyiv-based furniture and object design brand [that] specialises in creating original furniture, decor, and accessories for residential and commercial spaces.

“The first collaboration between Kint x Gushka, initiated in 2024, brings together contemporary furniture design and traditional Ukrainian craftsmanship. The result is a limited-edition series of armchairs, reimagining kint’s signature design through natural Carpathian wool and Gushka’s traditional textile techniques.

“The two versions feature different handcrafted finishes – Stranded uses hand-applied wool strands layered over a smooth base to create a distinctive textured surface, and Brushed is made by hand-combing wool using a traditional smooth-weaving technique, resulting in a softer texture.”

“KosKa is a Ukrainian brand working with recycled paper-based biomass, combining traditional handcrafting techniques, material experimentation, and contemporary artistic expression.

“Founder Kateryna Kostevych creates each object by hand, exploring the possibilities of sustainable materials and bringing together natural textures, tactile qualities, contemporary forms, and functionality.

“The featured objects include Trypillian Bull, an original interpretation of ancient Trypillian ceramic figurines, and two lamps named Hat and Bright Eye.”

“Tiini is a Ukrainian brand that creates lighting, furniture, and accessories, born at the intersection of tradition and modernity.

“The brand breathes new life into authentic crafts, harnessing the richness of materials and their interaction with light to create unique pieces for the home.”

“Venko is a Ukrainian design and production workshop founded in 2014 in Radyvyliv.

“The brand specialises in creating three-dimensional wooden wall panels and decorative pieces, with a particular focus on textures and the expressive qualities of natural materials.”

“Yalanzhi Objects is a Ukrainian brand of lighting and decorative objects founded in 2019 by Yuliia and Yevhen Melnychenko. The brand approaches light as an artistic medium, not merely a functional element, but a way to shape spaces, establish rhythm, and create an emotional focal point within an interior.

“Many of its pieces are crafted from Zemletsvit, the brand’s signature biocomposite – a natural material characterised by tactile surfaces, earthy tones, and a distinct handmade quality.

“Yalanzhi Objects combines contemporary design language, sculptural forms, and a thoughtful connection to Ukrainian culture.”

Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week 2026 takes place from 5 to 11 October 2026 at various locations in Kyiv, Ukraine. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

Picture this: you're stepping off a direct overnight flight at Dublin Airport, passport in hand, ready to spend two weeks exploring Ireland's Wild Atlantic Way — and the transatlantic crossing that would have cost you $600 per seat cost you just 13,000 Avios instead. That's the moment this redemption delivers. For the ChooseFI community, the math here is almost offensive in how good it is. A round-trip economy ticket from Boston to Dublin on Aer Lingus typically runs $300–$600 per person, and during peak summer travel it can climb even higher. At 13,000 Avios one-way, you're squeezing **2.3 to 4.6 cents per point** out of every Avios you redeem. To put that in perspective, most loyalty program analysts consider 1.5 cents per point a solid redemption. You're potentially tripling that benchmark on what is genuinely one of the easiest award bookings in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. The pricing inefficiency here runs deep. British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart** — meaning the price in Avios is determined by how many miles the plane physically flies, not by what the airline thinks the market will bear on that route. The North Atlantic crossing from the U.S. East Coast to Ireland is, by aviation standards, a relatively short haul. Dublin sits closer to Boston than Los Angeles does. That geographic reality, baked into BA's award chart structure, means you pay a "short-haul" price for what most travelers consider a major international trip. Aer Lingus operates modern Airbus A321LR aircraft on these transatlantic routes — a genuine premium product in economy with dedicated transatlantic seating, meal service, and that unmistakably warm Irish hospitality. This isn't a cramped regional jet. You're flying a purpose-built transatlantic cabin at a fraction of the cash cost. For a family of four, this redemption is transformational. At 13,000 Avios per person each way, a family round trip costs 104,000 Avios total — a points balance that's achievable with a single well-timed credit card welcome bonus. The alternative? Dropping $2,400 or more in cash for the same four seats. That's real money that stays in your FI journey.

The core insight here is understanding what British Airways Avios actually prices — and exploiting the gap between that and what the market charges.

BA's Avios program uses a distance-based award chart. Every flight is assigned a price based on the number of miles between the origin and destination, broken into distance bands. The critical band for this redemption is the one covering flights up to approximately 2,000 miles for partner airlines. Boston (BOS) to Dublin (DUB) clocks in at roughly 3,100 miles — but here's where it gets interesting: Aer Lingus prices these transatlantic short-haul routes within a favorable partner tier that makes the Avios cost dramatically lower than you'd ever pay booking directly.

Layer 1 — You're not booking BA flights. You're using BA Avios to book Aer Lingus flights. This distinction is everything. British Airways-operated long-haul flights carry notoriously high fuel surcharges — often $300–$800 or more on top of the Avios cost, which can completely destroy the value of your redemption. Aer Lingus, as a partner airline, charges no fuel surcharges on Avios bookings. You pay the Avios plus modest government taxes and fees, typically $5–$30. That's it.

Layer 2 — Off-peak pricing drops it further. BA Avios has off-peak pricing for Aer Lingus transatlantic routes, and when you travel in shoulder season, the rate can be even more favorable. The ChooseFI community travels smart: avoiding peak summer crowds and booking shoulder seasons isn't just about lower prices, it's about a better experience overall.

The instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Bilt mean you can search for availability, confirm your seats, then transfer points — no need to speculatively move points weeks in advance. That flexibility is a significant advantage for planning.

One important program nuance: Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. As long as you earn or redeem at least once every three years, your balance stays alive. For most ChooseFI members who hold a Chase or Amex card and regularly earn points, this is a non-issue — but it's worth knowing before you let a balance sit dormant.

Before transferring a single point, verify that award space actually exists on your target dates. Aer Lingus displays Avios availability directly on their website — look for the "Avios" fare option when selecting your flight. Alternatively, log into your British Airways Executive Club account at ba.com and use their award search tool. Search for Aer Lingus flights between your U.S. city and Dublin. The results will show Avios pricing — what you're looking for is the off-peak rate, which will display as lower Avios than the standard/peak option.

Use the BA award calendar view to spot off-peak pricing. Generally, traveling outside of peak summer (late June through August) and major holidays will unlock the best Avios rates. Shoulder seasons — late September through November and February through mid-April — are where the ChooseFI community finds the sweet spot of lower crowds, lower prices, and still-beautiful Irish weather.

#8863. 7 Common Misdiagnoses for Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS)

Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a skin condition that often gets caught up in a case of mistaken identity in a lineup of suspects. Specifically, people confuse HS for some more common conditions.

With their host of bumps, rashes, flakiness, or scales, skin conditions can sometimes be tricky to diagnose. That’s because they often share common symptoms or have symptoms that overlap with or mimic those of another skin issue.

So, what exactly is HS? It’s a chronic, progressive skin condition that typically appears as boil-like lumps in friction-prone and sweaty areas, where your skin can be sensitive. These lumps can form interconnected tracts underneath your skin (aka “tunneling”) that may become irritated or even infected.

Knowing how the symptoms of HS compare with those of other inflammatory skin conditions can help you advocate for the correct diagnosis and care, which is crucial for staving off disease progression.

Here are 7 conditions that HS commonly gets mistaken for.

HS isn’t rare — it affects up to 4% of the population. But by comparison, acne vulgaris affects more than more than 9% of people worldwide. Sometimes HS can be mistaken for acne simply because acne is more common. But these two conditions are quite different.

Acne typically shows up as papules, pustules, or nodules, which are commonly called zits or blemishes. Acne most often appears on your face but can also affect your back, chest, arms, and buttocks. It occurs when your sebaceous glands have a hypersensitivity to circulating androgens (like testosterone).

By comparison, HS most often appears in sweat- and friction-prone areas, such as your armpits or groin. It occurs when hair follicles become blocked — though more research is needed to learn what causes these blockages.

Acne conglobata (AC) is a rare but intense form of nodulocystic acne. With AC, the cysts and nodules connect under your skin, and this can lead to infections and scarring. Since AC features a “tunneling” effect that may appear similar to HS, many people confuse these two otherwise distinct conditions.

One key difference? HS often appears in areas that are subjected to friction from skin-on-skin contact or chafing. AC, on the other hand, can appear anywhere on your body. To further complicate things, many people with HS also have AC, and some research suggests a link between the two conditions.

A cyst is a fluid-filled sac. Cysts have many possible causes, including injuries and minor infections. They often go away on their own, but some may require treatment.

HS bumps can resemble cysts — but HS is an ongoing inflammatory condition.

An ingrown hair happens when a strand of hair anywhere on your body grows into your skin instead of out. Ingrown hairs commonly occur after shaving, waxing, or tweezing. After hair removal, a tiny new hair can curl inward, creating a bump (often called a razor bump).

Sometimes people confuse HS bumps for ingrown hairs — especially since HS often occurs in places where hair removal is common, such as the armpits and bikini area. Another confusing factor is that HS develops from blocked follicles. However, the cause of the blockage in HS is more complicated than an ingrown hair.

Folliculitis is inflammation of hair follicles, usually caused by a bacterial infection. The inflamed hair follicles show up as small bumps and can look like ingrown hairs.

People commonly mistake HS for folliculitis because the conditions often occur in the same skin areas.

Mild folliculitis tends to go away on its own with at-home treatment, though more severe forms may require antibiotics. HS, on the other hand, is a chronic condition.

A boil (also called a furuncle) is a bump filled with pus. The bump develops from a bacterial infection, often of a hair follicle. The infection causes a buildup of immune and skin cells, which leads to the formation of the bump. A carbuncle is a cluster of boils.

People often confuse HS with boils. However, boils are the result of an infection, and proper treatment typically resolves the issue. Meanwhile, the boil-like bumps of HS often require ongoing treatment.

Herpes is a common sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the herpes simplex virus. It shows up as painful sores or blisters.

Since herpes often affects the genital area and HS occurs around the groin or bikini line, people may confuse the two conditions. But while herpes can be spread through direct contact, HS is not contagious.

Other skin conditions can mimic HS, and vice versa. But a misdiagnosis can lead to an incorrect treatment that won’t actually ease your symptoms or slow the condition’s progression. This is true for other skin conditions as well.

That’s why, if you have symptoms of any of the above conditions, you should talk with a knowledgeable dermatologist who can properly diagnose your concerns and find the right treatment plan.

Last medically reviewed on February 14, 2025

#8862. Latin America in Focus: This Month in Architecture, Social Housing, and Heritage Recovery

This October, architecture across Latin America became a platform for exchange, bringing together discussions on inhabitation, cultural identity, emerging practices, and the relationship between the built environment and its wider context. From conversations on emerging architectural practices and material research at Design Week Mexico to new approaches to housing, landscape, and public space in Chile and Mexico, recent developments highlight how architecture responds to specific local conditions. Across the region, initiatives addressing climate adaptation and heritage recovery in the Dominican Republic and Colombia also bring attention to the changing responsibilities of cultural institutions and the built environment.

Architecture as a Platform for Exchange: Biennials, Design, and Emerging Practices Across Latin America

The 20th Buenos Aires International Architecture Biennial brought architecture into a broader conversation about inhabitation, examining how social, cultural, environmental, and political conditions shape the ways people live. Held under the curatorial theme INHABIT, the event brought together international lectures, exhibitions, and public activities across six main venues and partner institutions, with contributions from architects including Smiljan Radić, Solano Benitez, Andrés Jaque, and Marina Otero Verzier. Through discussions on memory, materiality, urban development, and the relationship between architecture and its context, the Biennial positioned inhabitation as a framework for understanding architecture's role in shaping contemporary societies. Its exhibitions and public program continued throughout October as part of Buenos Aires Design and Architecture Month, extending the exchange beyond the International Forum and into the city's cultural institutions.

In Mexico City, Design Week Mexico 2026 explored the relationship between identity, craftsmanship, and contemporary design, with Chile participating as Guest Country of Honor and an ongoing collaboration between Mexican artisans and French designers continuing through its intercultural residency program. The event also provided the setting for ArchDaily's Next Practices Live in Mexico, hosted at Design House during the opening week of Design Week Mexico. Moderated by ArchDaily Editor-in-Chief Christele Harrouk, the conversation brought together 2026 Next Practices Awards winners MANUFACTURA, RAMA Estudio, and SOCA, alongside previous Mexican winners ASPJ and Palma, to discuss how emerging practices are expanding architecture's agency through material research, ecological knowledge, cultural engagement, and responses to specific social and environmental conditions.

Santa Rosa Social Housing / FAR frohn&rojas

Located along Avenida Santa Rosa in central Santiago, Santa Rosa Social Housing by FAR frohn&rojas explores an alternative approach to social housing by integrating residential units into the city's existing transportation and social infrastructure. Completed in 2026, the 2,337-square-meter project occupies an exceptionally narrow site, measuring less than nine meters wide, which informed the development of a seven-story building organized around a slender concrete structure. Most apartments are duplex units accessed through shared galleries, with living spaces opening onto circulation areas and bedrooms positioned on the upper levels. A perforated blue metal screen provides shading while preserving the expression of the raw concrete structure, and shared verandas introduce communal outdoor spaces. Developed through Chile's DS-49 social housing program, the project also incorporates a strategy to support the long-term maintenance of shared amenities through advertising revenue generated by its north-facing façade.

Located on the outskirts of Guadalajara, Mexico, Rancho del Abuelo by Mendiola Arregui is a 994-square-meter equestrian complex completed in 2026 that brings together facilities for horse care, recreation, and gathering within an existing landscape. The project is organized as a series of independent pavilions positioned in response to the site's existing conditions, with a shared architectural system connecting their different programs. Flat concrete roofs supported by columns establish a consistent structural framework, while independent walls define individual spaces and shape circulation, framing views of the landscape and surrounding trees. The separation between the roofs and walls allows natural light and ventilation to permeate the complex, creating a sequence of pathways, courtyards, and shaded areas.

Located along the Loncomilla River in San Javier de Loncomilla, Chile, Urban Mantle by Felipe Burgos Villablanca is a 16-square-meter public installation that seeks to reconnect the city with its riverfront and historical landscape. Developed as a contemplative seating structure, the project responds to the site's former role in colonial maritime trade and its gradual disconnection from the urban fabric. A curved concrete surface accommodates different resting positions, transforming an informal riverside gathering area into a space for rest, meditation, and landscape observation. Drawing on the work of Enric Miralles and Anne Holtrop, the design combines an organic form with a material approach that embraces the construction process and its imperfections.

Santo Domingo Tests UNESCO Climate Action Toolkit for Historic Heritage

The Colonial City of Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic became the first cultural World Heritage property in Latin America and the Caribbean to pilot UNESCO's Climate Action Toolkit. Held from October 5 to 9, the workshop brought together heritage conservation, urban planning, and disaster risk management specialists to assess how hurricanes, heavy rainfall, and flooding could affect the historic center. Developed by UNESCO alongside ICCROM, ICOMOS, and IUCN, the toolkit connects climate projections and local knowledge with heritage management and planning strategies. The pilot will contribute to the development of a climate action plan for the historic district, highlighting the importance of integrating climate preparedness into the conservation of living urban heritage.

Colombia Mobilizes Cultural Institutions to Support Post-Earthquake Heritage Recovery

Following the August 10 earthquake, which affected cultural heritage across seven Colombian departments, several institutions launched initiatives in October to support recovery efforts. On October 6, the National Museum of Colombia, ICOM Colombia, and Universidad Externado de Colombia established a collection center in Bogotá to gather restoration materials for affected museums. The initiative followed reports of damage at 35 museums and museum institutions across 10 departments. Meanwhile, the District Institute of Cultural Heritage (IDPC) continued its volunteer program, carrying out architectural surveys, photographic documentation, and preliminary damage assessments in affected municipalities. These efforts form part of a broader recovery process led by cultural institutions and public authorities to assess damage, protect collections, and safeguard the country's architectural heritage.

#8861. Why BIM Still Doesn't Know What Your Building Is Made Of

Move a wall in Revit and every plan, section and schedule follows. Change a material, though, and the team is often back in specifications, spreadsheets and drawings, checking that they all describe the same choice.

Move a wall in Revit and every plan, section and schedule follows. Change a material, though, and the team is often back in specifications, spreadsheets and drawings, checking that they all describe the same choice.

For Dave Lemont, who led Revit Technology before Autodesk acquired it, that gap is BIM's unfinished work. Now Executive Chairman of Acelab, he is focused on a Material Intelligence Model: one structured product record, connected to every document where that selection appears. It is also something architects can now try for themselves, since Acelab has opened Material Hub search to anyone, no account required.

Now Executive Chairman of Acelab, he is focused on a Material Intelligence Model: one structured product record, connected to every document where that selection appears. In this conversation, he discusses what connected material data means for architects and owners, where AI helps, and why the final call still belongs to the designer.

Eduardo Souza (ArchDaily): When you were bringing Revit to market, what did you hope to change about architectural practice?

Eduardo Souza (ArchDaily): When you were bringing Revit to market, what did you hope to change about architectural practice?

Dave Lemont (Acelab): Everything was 2D. The plan, section, elevation and schedule were drawn separately, as unrelated drawings that happened to describe the same building. Move a

Dave Lemont (Acelab): Everything was 2D. The plan, section, elevation and schedule were drawn separately, as unrelated drawings that happened to describe the same building. Move a

wall and someone had to find it again in each one and change it by hand. The breakthrough was the parametric building model: one model, with every drawing as a view of it. Change the model and the drawings update; edit a drawing and the model updates. The name Revit came from "revise instantly." The larger idea, which later took the name BIM, was that a building could be represented as intelligent objects carrying all the material information, not just geometry.

Change the model and the drawings update; edit a drawing and the model updates. The name Revit came from "revise instantly." The larger idea, which later took the name BIM, was that a building could be represented as intelligent objects carrying all the material information, not just geometry.

The drawings agreed only because a person made them agree.

The drawings agreed only because a person made them agree.

AD: Why is material information still so difficult to connect across tools and documents?

AD: Why is material information still so difficult to connect across tools and documents?

DL: Because nothing connects a material's attributes to all the documents that describe it. The information lives across models, specs, PDFs, spreadsheets and manufacturer sites, and someone moves it between them by hand.

DL: Because nothing connects a material's attributes to all the documents that describe it. The information lives across models, specs, PDFs, spreadsheets and manufacturer sites, and someone moves it between them by hand.

Take a porcelain tile selected early in design. It goes into the schedule under one name, the spec under the manufacturer's product line, and a keynote under shorthand typed before a deadline. Months later the contractor prices the spec, the tile has a sixteen-week lead time, and the approved substitute never makes it back into the drawings. Every document reflects a different stage of the decision, and nothing keeps them aligned.This results in costly errors and change orders.

Material intelligence, and search anyone can use

AD: What led you from BIM to material intelligence, and how do the two connect?

AD: What led you from BIM to material intelligence, and how do the two connect?

DL: I kept watching the same gap persist from the Revit days. BIM gave architects a coordinated model of geometry, then left them to make the highest-consequence decisions, the material selections, off the platform in PDFs and phone calls.

DL: I kept watching the same gap persist from the Revit days. BIM gave architects a coordinated model of geometry, then left them to make the highest-consequence decisions, the material selections, off the platform in PDFs and phone calls.

Material intelligence gives every product selection the treatment Revit gave geometry. We call it the Material Information Model: a single structured record carrying the material's full attribute set, connected to every document where it appears. Make the selection once and the schedule, spec, keynote and drawing all draw from the same source. Join that to the building model and you get what I call material-forward design, where choosing materials is part of designing rather than a chore that comes afterward.

AD: Performance, cost, availability and environmental impact pull in different directions. How can a system help architects compare them without suggesting one "best" material?

AD: Performance, cost, availability and environmental impact pull in different directions. How can a system help architects compare them without suggesting one "best" material?

DL: The best material selection is not always what was chosen before. The right answer changes by project, client and region. What a system can do is make the trade-offs visible on a common basis. We normalized product data into one schema, so every product can be compared side by side, including HPDs, EPDs, certifications and code requirements. Our AI assistant ACE will lay out comparisons, analyze lessons learned from past projects and make recommendations but the judgment remains with the architect.

What it changes for owners and architects

AD: Where does the return show up, for owners and for the design team?

AD: Where does the return show up, for owners and for the design team?

DL: It comes from every stakeholder working from the same record early, when decisions are still inexpensive to change. Materials cost 50% of every building, yet owners rarely see those selections while they're being made. With one source, they can see what's selected, at what cost and against what standard, in real time. A choice that's over budget or off the owner's standard gets caught at selection, not in a change order months later.

Architects gain too. Documentation generated from a coordinated source cuts the last-minute discrepancies teams fix for free. And when a contractor proposes a value-engineering alternative, it's checked against the original criteria on the spot, so the cheaper option still meets what the project required.

DL: Adding more data fields is easy. The hard part is knowing which attributes matter for a given decision. Fire rating matters on a corridor ceiling. Acoustic performance matters in a classroom.

That's the work Ace, our AI assistant in Material Hub, is doing today. It reasons across performance data, code requirements and a firm's project history at once, flags what needs an expert's eye, and connects a choice to its consequences downstream. It also catches errors and inconsistencies in the data, because bad data in a decision system is worse than none: people act on it.

Architects are right to resist being scored. Selection draws on precedent, visual judgment and instinct no algorithm has. A good tool doesn't rank products. It puts the data, visual reference, cost and the firm's own history with a product side by side, with sources visible, so the architect makes the call with everything in view.

DL: More data is worth adding only when it changes a decision. If it lets someone choose better, coordinate better or defend a choice, it earns its place. If it only makes the model heavier, it's a liability. So decide what question you're answering, then carry only the information that answers it. Some of the most valuable data is the firm's own. Every project teaches something about which products performed, which caused RFIs and which a client asked never to see again. Today that knowledge lives in people's heads and old project folders, and it leaves when people do. Our AI works from our product catalog alongside a firm's or owner's past project data and standards, so each project starts from what the organization already learned.
